topic: The Mystery of Pi in the Normal Distribution: The Gaussian Integral

outline.topic: The Mystery of Pi in the Normal Distribution: The Gaussian Integral

sections.title: The Hook: Why Pi?
sections.content: Introduce the Normal Distribution curve (the bell curve). State the paradox: the function involves the exponential of a square, yet its area integrates to exactly 1. We pose the question: where does the transcendental number π emerge from when there are no circles involved?
sections.example: Visualize a target practice scenario: archer 'Artie' shoots arrows that cluster around the bullseye. The probability density function describes his accuracy, featuring the mysterious constant π.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Gaussian Integral
sections.content: Define the target integral: I = ∫ e^(-x²) dx from -∞ to +∞. Explain that the anti-derivative of e^(-x²) cannot be expressed in elementary functions, necessitating a clever geometric trick.
sections.example: An animation showing a flat 1D line transforming into a 2D plane to create a 'mountain' shape (a 3D Gaussian surface).

sections.title: The Geometric Bridge: Polar Coordinates
sections.content: Explain the trick: Square the integral (I²) to create a double integral over the entire plane. Convert from Cartesian coordinates (dx dy) to Polar coordinates (r dr dθ). This introduces the 'r' factor from the Jacobian, which allows for simple u-substitution.
sections.example: Visual transition: A square grid map changing into a circular radar screen. The 'r' appearing from nowhere is highlighted as the 'key' that unlocks the integral.

sections.title: The Calculation: Unveiling π
sections.content: Demonstrate the integration of 2πr * e^(-r²) dr. Show how the integral of r*e^(-r²) is easily solved, and the integration of dθ simply yields 2π. The result I² = π confirms I = √π.
sections.example: Animation showing the integration slice by slice sweeping around the center, naturally accumulating the full circle (2π).

sections.title: Synthesis and Conclusion
sections.content: Connect back to the Normal Distribution: The normalization constant (1/√(2πσ²)) exists specifically to ensure the total area under the bell curve is 1. Summarize that π appears because the bell curve is a rotationally symmetric object in 2D space.
sections.example: A 3D bell-shaped 'tent' being dropped over a 2D plane; the 'circle' hidden in the base of the tent explains the presence of π in the probability formula.

storyboard.title: The Hook: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: The bell curve is everywhere in statistics.
But why does π appear in its formula?
Circles are absent; it seems like a mystery.
animations: Display Gaussian integral $I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} dx$ in center. Text: #FFFFFF.
Flash "Non-elementary" in red (#FF0000) below the integral.
Show circle radius increasing with time to hint at geometry.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Gaussian Integral
lecture_lines: We need a clever trick to solve it.
animations: Write $I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} dx$ in the center. Color: #FFFFFF.
Write $I^2 = (\int e^{-x^2} dx) (\int e^{-y^2} dy)$. Color: #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Bridge: Polar Coordinates
lecture_lines: Square the integral to create a 2D plane.
Switch to polar coordinates: r, dr, and dθ.
The factor 'r' appears as the key.
animations: Show 2D coordinate plane with axes. Color: #808080.
Draw a circle of radius r. Color: #FFA500. Add label 'r'.
Show the transformation: $dx dy = r dr d\theta$. Color: #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: The Calculation: Unveiling π
lecture_lines: Integrate over the full circular plane.
Solving this confirms the integral is √π.
animations: Show polar integral $\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r dr d\theta$. Color: #FFFFFF.
Show final result $\sqrt{\pi}$ in a box. Color: #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: Synthesis and Conclusion
lecture_lines: The bell curve has rotational symmetry.
That symmetry brings π into the formula.
animations: Rotate the surface to show symmetry. Color: #00FF00.
